title: Carrying On the Good Work of Others
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Admired Leadership uses the story of Terry Fox's Marathon of Hope to argue that a leader's highest value can lie in expanding a project's ownership rather than personally finishing it. The piece recounts how Fox, having lost part of his leg to bone cancer, set out to run across Canada on an artificial leg to raise money for cancer research, but had to stop after 143 days and 5,373 kilometers when the disease spread to his lungs; he died months later at 22. The turning point of the story is Isadore Sharp, the Four Seasons founder who had also lost a son to cancer, who saw that Fox's dream needed to continue without him and helped launch the annual Terry Fox Run, which drew 300,000 participants and raised $3.5 million in its first year alone. The piece uses the resulting Terry Fox Foundation, which has since raised more than $1 billion through over 9,000 annual events, as evidence that an initiative deliberately made to belong to many people becomes more durable than one that depends on its originator. Its central leadership lesson inverts a common assumption: leaders often believe their job is to finish what they start, but Fox's legacy suggests that building on and redistributing ownership of important work is an equally valuable, and sometimes more powerful, leadership act.
points: Terry Fox's Marathon of Hope stopped after 143 days and 5,373 kilometers when his cancer spread, but the initiative's real scale came only after his death, through the Terry Fox Run that Isadore Sharp helped launch.

The Terry Fox Foundation has since raised more than $1 billion, with over 9,000 annual events, illustrating what happens when an initiative is deliberately designed to belong to a community rather than one person.
Admired Leadership reframes the standard assumption that a leader's job is to finish what they start, arguing that making an initiative belong to many others is often the more valuable, durable move.
Isadore Sharp's role, spotting Fox's unfinished work and building the infrastructure to carry it forward, is presented as its own form of leadership distinct from originating the idea.
The piece's takeaway is that expanding an idea's ownership, not personally completing it, is what makes a great initiative 'nearly unstoppable.'
quotes: He decided to run across Canada on an artificial leg to raise money for cancer research. He called it the Marathon of Hope.
Terry understood that the Marathon of Hope couldn't depend on just himself. He wanted Canadians to continue it without him.
He helped launch the Terry Fox Run in 1981 at more than 760 locations in Canada and around the world. In that first year, more than 300,000 people participated and raised more than $3.5 million.

His real achievement wasn't completing the run but in convincing millions of people that they could pick up something unfinished and carry it forward. Thanks to the leadership of Isadore Sharp, that's exactly what happened.
Leaders often think their job is to finish what they start. Terry Fox's legacy suggests something equally valuable: building on the important work of others.

If leadership is about making people and situations better, then expanding the influence of a great idea is what good leaders do. Terry Fox proved that a project embraced and taken up by a vast community becomes nearly unstoppable.
